auto_summary: Deep technical review of p95/p99 behavior across streaming vs non-streaming modes. Focus on network hop variability, KV cache hit patterns for long-context workloads, batching tradeoffs, and quantization impact on latency. Identified likely network-induced p99 spikes and plan for controlled benching on a dedicated pool, plus follow-ups around VPC peering and prompt corpus for realistic tests.

transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I want to dive right into the p99 behavior you reported last week, especially during streaming responses. Priya will run the bench with you.
[00:21] Evan: Cool, yeah we've been seeing consistent p95 around 160ms but p99 jumps to 1.1s sporadically, feels like tail spikes when the context is long or during bursts.
[00:37] Priya: okay, first question, are you using streaming on the client and server both? And is the client reassembly introducing delays?
[00:47] Marisol: we're streaming from your hosted API, client is a Node SSE handler, but we've ruled out client-side thread blocking. Network team says some requests go through extra hops to our central VPC.
[01:05] Alex: that extra hop can add tens to hundreds ms, especially if TLS handshakes or NAT gateways are in play. Have you mapped the egress path?
[01:18] Marisol: not fully, we have the diagram but will share it — there's an AWS transit gateway in the path.
[01:27] Jordan: great, please share. On the server side, streaming keeps the encoder/decoder path open and incremental tokens flush; that can surface mid-request variations. With streaming, p99 can be amplified by a single long tail token generation or a backend VM spin event.
[01:47] Evan: We also saw p99 correlate with cold KV cache conditions per our logs — when a conversation references older context the KV hit rate drops. Is that expected?
[01:58] Priya: yes, KV cache warmup matters a lot. If your workload has long-tail prefixes, the runtime may need to recompute attention keys and load from disk-backed cache for the oldest segments, adding latency. Our continuous batching and prefix caching help but you need stable working set.
[02:18] Evan: The model is a 70B open-arch variant, quantized to 4-bit using your suggested profile. Could quant at 4-bit cause micro stalls?
[02:30] Priya: quantization changes memory access patterns; 4-bit is usually fine but some kernels do an unpack/pack step that can cost a few ms per token. Under heavy load those per-token costs stack and affect p99. For streaming, that cost shows up earlier because tokens are flushed frequently.
[02:52] Tom B.: So is the recommendation to move to non-streaming for lower p99?
[02:58] Alex: not always — non-streaming can save on TCP/TLS overhead but increases latency at the first byte since you wait for full generation. Streaming lowers median latency and perceived responsiveness, but tail depends on per-token stalls. There's no one-size-fits-all.
[03:16] Priya: for p99 reduction we recommend: 1) dedicated nodes to reduce variance, 2) controlled batching policy (max batch wait < 5ms) and dynamic batching thresholds, 3) ensure KV working set fits in memory or pre-warm during ramp, 4) consider mixed precision quant profiles tuned per-layer.
[03:36] Evan: When you say dedicated, do you mean Redwood Dedicated reserved pool? We have compliance needs and might do Private too.
[03:43] Jordan: Dedicated gives you isolation and consistent noisy-neighbor behavior — less p99 variance. Private (VPC/on-prem) adds network considerations but you control peering. For on-prem the network hop is internal so you avoid internet jitter but you could have internal infra noise — we run the same runtime in both.
[04:02] Marisol: our infra team worried about packet flow through the transit gateway causing spikes. Any mitigations?
[04:09] Priya: Reroute egress via direct peering or use persistent connections with keep-alive and TLS session reuse; also use our regional endpoints to reduce hops. We can share a peering checklist.
[04:23] Evan: How do you measure p99 in a way that's meaningful? We use service-level p99 for perceived latency and also token-level p99 in dashboards.
[04:33] Jordan: recommended: measurement at the client edge for end-to-end p99, and server-side breakdown per stage: queue wait, kernel execution, KV fetch, postprocess. Redwood Console traces token-level timings which helps isolate whether p99 is network, cache, or kernel-related.
[04:50] Tom B.: I want to understand batching tradeoffs — we saw larger batches reduce cost but increase p95 and p99.
[04:59] Alex: exactly; batching increases throughput but molecularly increases latency per request because you wait to fill a batch or hit timeout. We recommend adaptive batching: small cap for latency-sensitive routes and larger batch for background/low-priority requests. Also route-by-policy, separate critical traffic to dedicated lanes.
[05:18] Evan: Any knobs to tune on the runtime side?
[05:22] Priya: yes — kernel selection, KV sharding, batch wait thresholds, max batch size, and quant profile per model. For p99 you can lower max batch wait to 1-3ms and pin latency-critical routes to hot workers with reserved slots. Also enable prefix caching aggressively for dialog flows.
[05:45] Marisol: Is there visibility into per-token kernel times? If we see one token that takes 200ms it could be a kernel fallback.
[05:54] Jordan: Console provides per-route histograms and raw traces; we can instrument a few requests and share flamegraph-like timing. Note transcription: sometimes traces show "kernel fallback" events when a preferred SIMD kernel isn't available and it uses a compatibility path — that's often a p99 culprit.
[06:14] Evan: Okay. For the bench you mentioned, can you replicate our long context? We have 16K token conversations.
[06:22] Priya: yes, we'll run a synthetic trace with your 16K context and the three long prompts you provide. We'll run streaming and non-streaming variants, dedicated pool config, and quant profiles (4-bit, 8-bit float sim) to compare.
[06:36] Tom B.: Any impact of TLS termination on p99? We're terminating at the transit gateway sometimes.
[06:42] Alex: TLS at the edge adds CPU overhead and can cause short bursts of latency if session reuse isn't configured. Offload TLS where possible or use persistent connections. Also watch for NAT gateway cold translations.
[06:56] Marisol: We also saw a correlation with autoscaler activity — when new nodes join p99 spikes briefly. Is that expected?
[07:04] Priya: autoscale events cause temporary routing changes and cold caches; Dedicated with some headroom or warm standby nodes reduces that. We have graceful rollout policies to avoid disruptive scale-ins.
[07:18] Evan: For quantization, which layers usually cause fallback penalties?
[07:23] Priya: some attention kernels and rotary embeddings have optimized paths for certain data layouts; if quantization changes layout you may fall back to slower code paths. We can share a layer-level heatmap from our profiler.
[07:37] Jordan: quick recap of actionables: Priya will run the 10k p99 bench with streaming and non-streaming, dedicated node config and quant profiles. Evan will send prompt corpus and network diagram. Jordan sends pricing and peering checklist.
[07:51] Marisol: sounds good. Also we'd like a short doc on recommended batch configs for conversational vs single-shot generation.
[07:58] Jordan: we'll draft that.
[08:01] Speaker 4: (brief crosstalk) yeah the bench should include heavy concurrent sessions to emulate real traffic.
[08:10] Alex: one more tip: for tails, consider token-level early cutoff / partial responses for non-critical tokens, that sometimes avoids waiting on problematic tokens.
[08:22] Evan: interesting, we'll test that.
[08:25] Jordan: ok we'll follow up in the next sync with bench results. Thanks everyone.
[08:30] (meeting ends)
notes: Transcript contains minor ASR errors like 'KV cash' vs KV cache and occasional speaker mislabels.
Measured p95 ~160ms, reported p99 ~1.1s in customer logs; likely combined network + cache miss + quant kernel fallback causes.
